title: The evolution of artificial intelligence talent demand in China: Evidence from large-scale online job posting data
locator: ScienceDirect public Abstract and Highlights; directly opened in browser 2026-10-19. One-to-five-year experience and postgraduate requirements in Abstract.
summary: Authors report more selective AI recruitment and increased education and experience requirements in Chinese postings from 2018–2025.
appraisal: The public abstract and preview were inspected directly on ScienceDirect. The article attributes only what that abstract reports; it does not validate methods or infer causation. Full paper remains access-restricted. Ads are not hires or all graduate employment.
inspection_scope: Public abstract and publisher preview only. Full text and complete methods NOT inspected.

title: Novel AI Technologies and the Future of Work in Malaysia
authors: Calvin Cheng; Hanson Chong; Matthew Dornan; Alyssa Farha Jasmin
locator: PDF pages 9–11,15–17 (one-based); Figure6–7 on PDF page17 visually inspected; 2021 LFS mapping
summary: Models Malaysian occupational exposure and raises a risk to progression into skilled work. Highest-exposure shares peak at ages 25–34; ages 15–24 are most represented in the lowest-exposure quartile.
appraisal: MASCO tasks scored with GPT-4o, linked to LFS. Static task feasibility, not observed adoption, displacement or hiring. Explicitly agnostic about replacement versus complementarity; cannot directly capture new job creation. Age bands are not Gen Z or experience measures. Chart percentages visually checked against original PDF. Employment composition is from 2021.

title: Automation anxiety: New AI technologies and employment outcomes in Malaysia
publisher: Centre for Responsible Technology / ISIS Malaysia
locator: Sections 2.2–2.3; 3.3 age results; Technical Appendix A1 interpretation and A2 strata
summary: Reports higher employment-loss measures in more AI-exposed Malaysian occupations, including a positive association for ages 25–34.
appraisal: PERKESO/EIS formal private-sector separations, not first-job hiring. Main occupation-month analysis 2023–2025 with fixed 2021 LFS denominators. No firm-level adoption; cross-sectional conditional exposure gradient, expressly non-causal. Subgroup denominators are not stratum-specific. Ages 15–24 do not show a significant positive association. Shares index derives from S3: related, not independent exposure validation. Avoid headline risk percentages.

title: Why AI Is Not (Yet) Behind Malaysia’s Job Losses
locator: Why the attribution of job losses to AI is premature; Measure better; references
summary: Argues that exposure-based associations cannot attribute Malaysian retrenchments to AI without adoption and linked worker-outcome data.
appraisal: Primary source for Rosli’s methodological argument; commentary, not a new causal employment study. Discusses S3/S4 and other studies, so repeated evidence is not independent replication. Do not adopt its reported retrenchment totals without inspecting underlying records.

title: Generative AI at Work
publisher: Quarterly Journal of Economics / Oxford University Press
authors: Erik Brynjolfsson; Danielle Li; Lindsey Raymond
locator: Abstract; III.B; IV.B; V.B.3 and FigureV narrative; final licensing paragraph; IV.A rollout timing rechecked22October2026
summary: A staggered workplace rollout across 5,172 customer-support agents found larger gains for less-experienced and lower-skilled workers.
appraisal: Peer-reviewed field study; primarily Philippines-based support for a US software firm. Non-random rollout with identification checks, not a randomized graduate-hiring experiment. Productivity and learning of employed agents do not establish increased entry hiring or universal benefits. Learning-time chart preserves authors approximate narrative:2 versus8–10 months, not an exact estimated target time.
reference_period: Rollout mainly autumn2020 and winter2021; paper published February2025. These dates are rollout timing, not a claimed full sample window.

title: Who Will Become the Next Senior? How Generative AI Erodes the Development Pathway in Software Engineering
publisher: arXiv preprint / Seoul National University authors
locator: Method: Study Design and Participants; Findings: Absorption; Limitations
summary: Fourteen South Korean interviews describe beginner tasks moving into senior-plus-AI workflows and concerns over lost learning opportunities.
appraisal: Eight junior and six senior participants recruited through networks. Exploratory qualitative accounts, not representative prevalence or causal identification. The revision reports only the participants' described task reassignment; no extrapolated senior-advantage model is adopted.

title: Employment Statistics, Second Quarter 2026
inspection_scope: Relevant passages and measurement limits listed in locator; no unreported forecast method or policy impact inferred.
locator: Introduction; Labour Demand by Skills Category; Labour Demand by Economic Activity. Full official HTML downloaded and inspected 22 October; corroborating DOSM two-page release file_20260813110950.pdf page 2.
summary: Q2 2026: 195.7k vacancies; semi-skilled107.3k, skilled50.2k, low-skilled38.2k. Manufacturing114.0k/58.3% of total.
appraisal: Quarterly Employment Survey among covered registered private-sector businesses, not whole economy. Rounded survey estimates, no uncertainty interval reported in overview. Occupational skill groups do not identify educational qualifications, age, new entrants, pay, reasons for vacancies or AI use. Sector and skill counts are two classifications of the same vacancies, not additive.

title: Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure
inspection_scope: Relevant passages and measurement limits listed in locator; no unreported forecast method or policy impact inferred.
locator: Introduction; sections 3.4,4–8; printed pp.29,38–39 (PDF pp.31,40–41); footnote18 equal task weights; section3.1 initial models available end2024
summary: Clerical occupations most exposed; manual-task exposure assessed lower. Worker ratings, expert review and AI predictions; equally weighted task scores.
appraisal: Data-based assessment of technological exposure published in May2025, with initial AI scoring from models available at the end of2024, not realised adoption or job-demand outcomes. Survey of 1640 employed Polish respondents plus expert judgments and LLM predictions. Most rated tasks were not performed by the respondent. Equal task weights because frequency/importance unavailable. Assumptions and ratings not established as observed automation probabilities. Global classification lacks local Malaysian nuance; not an index of all robotics/automation. No new model created here.
reference_period: Initial AI scoring: models available at end2024; classification validated1January2025. No precise survey fieldwork dates identified in inspected methods, so none invented.

title: Higher Education Statistics 2025, Chapter 7: Graduate Tracer Study
locator: PDF pp2,7 (one-based), printed pp210,215; Tables7.1/7.2 and7.7. Downloaded official PDF, text extracted and counts reconciled.
summary: KESUMA row:5367 employed,339 unemployed,n5706,94.1%; employee position:2501 permanent,1557 contract,513 temporary,123 part-time,n4694.
appraisal: Reference year2025, released directory14May2026. Malaysian graduate tracer respondents in labour force, not all graduates; position denominator equals government+private employees inTable7.6 (442+4252=4694), not all employed5367. Respondent selection/nonresponse cannot be appraised from chapter; no row response rates/CI supplied. Cross-sectional survey-time outcomes, no causal policy effect, job match/pay or AI attribution. TVET table2025 includes TVET MADANI programmes; do not splice its aggregate into2024 coverage. English column labels inspected.

title: Graduate Employment Rate — English definition
locator: Opening definition paragraphs before Year selector
summary: From2024 rate=employed/(employed+unemployed); status shortly after graduation. Prior employability includes study/training/waiting placement.
appraisal: Operational denominator excludes outside labour force; survey timing not long-term. Definition break prevents naive pre2024 employment trend. No invented fixed follow-up window.

title: MyMahir Malaysia Critical Occupations List (MyCOL)
locator: About header; MyCOL overview and Highlights01–04
summary: KESUMA agency/strategic thinktankMarch2024; MyCOL18sectors employer survey/direct engagement and regional shortages.
appraisal: Official programme description supports purpose/process only; does not evaluate placement effectiveness, fresh-graduate access or wage quality. Employer evidence not a census of all vacancies.

title: National Structured Internship Programme (MySIP)
locator: Overview; requirements; Options1/2 evaluation steps
summary: Structured practical modules include TVET, employer and intern evaluations.
appraisal: Design/existence not causal graduate outcome or demonstrated wage/retention impact. No tax advice or assertion internships guarantee jobs.

title: Impact Study of AI, Digital, and Green Economy on the Malaysian Workforce — English summary
locator: Summary final paragraphs: FSTC regular assessments, update roles; opening3–5year horizon
summary: Describes anticipated change and sector skills assessment/update process.
appraisal: Public English summary inspected; full model not appraised and numeric forward impact estimates deliberately excluded. Assessment terminology validated does not empirically validate future displacement.

title: China Economic Update — December2022
locator: Printed p37, Figure19 discussion and footnote8; printed pp37–38 mismatch/TVETcapacity discussion
summary: Graduate vacancy/application ratios1.6(2018–19) to1.0(2020–22); expanded college/TVET alongside mismatch concerns.
appraisal: English institutional research synthesis; platform evidence CIER/Zhaopin not national census, vacancy/application ratio not probability of employment. Pandemic/preGenAI period cannot identify later AI effects or evaluate2026forecast success. Correct publication December2022 (not URL indexing2023).

title: Canaries in the Coal Mine, August 2026 revision
publisher: Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen; Stanford Digital Economy Lab
authors: Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen; Stanford Digital Economy Lab
inspection_scope: Relevant full-text passages inspected, not every appendix
locator: Abstract; introduction; data section; hiring/separations analysis; education and national-data comparisons
summary: In the balanced payroll panel, employment at ages 22-25 fell about 11% in the top two AI-exposure quintiles and grew about 10% in the bottom three. Reduced hiring accounts for most of the difference.
appraisal: Descriptive, not causal. Age is not graduate status. Pre-existing trends, educational composition and sample coverage matter. The relative shortfall is not a count of jobs destroyed by AI.

title: How Does AI Change Labor Demand? Evidence from 41 Countries
publisher: Bharat Chandar and Bouke Klein Teeselink
authors: Bharat Chandar and Bouke Klein Teeselink
inspection_scope: Relevant empirical design, results and limitations inspected; structural model not adopted
locator: Printed pp. 2-6, 13-16, 26-27; Figure 7 definition of seniority
origin_group: Revelio records; overlapping Stanford author with F01, different underlying dataset
summary: Estimated junior employment share at adopting foreign affiliates is 1.9 percentage points below controls by March 2026, primarily through senior growth. Senior employment estimate +6.7%; junior -2.5%, not statistically significant.
appraisal: Working paper. Adoption inferred from job advertisements. Instrument assumes peer adoption near foreign headquarters affects affiliate employment only through company AI adoption. Tests cannot verify that assumption. Digitally attached multinationals, not representative national economies; junior is Revelio levels 1-2, not necessarily young graduates. No Malaysian estimate established. Structural decomposition and economy-wide model are excluded from our proposed claim.

title: Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI
locator: Abstract; printed pp. 1-4; section 3.4; Figure 8
origin_group: Danish adoption surveys linked to administrative records
summary: Across 11 exposed occupations, estimated average earnings and recorded-hours effects are close to zero, ruling out effects larger than 2%. No differential early-career employment-share decline at adopting workplaces; tasks reorganised.
appraisal: Observational difference-in-differences requires comparison assumptions. Ends in 2024; cannot describe later agent adoption. Average null effects do not establish safety for every occupation or person.

title: Written Answer to PQ on Trends in Job Vacancies
locator: Answer paragraphs 1-2
origin_group: Singapore MOM official vacancy and firm survey reporting
summary: Entry-level PMET vacancies increased from 32,500 to 32,800. Among AI-adopting firms, 6% reported headcount cuts, 8% reduced hiring, 19% role redesign and 14% creation of AI-related jobs.
appraisal: Vacancies are not completed hires. Survey shares concern firms, not workers, and must not be added as mutually exclusive categories. Short period; self-reported changes do not identify causal effects or graduate outcomes.
reference_period: Vacancies December 2025-March 2026; survey findings reported in August answer

title: The Early Impacts of AI on Employment among Recent College Graduates
publisher: Robert Fairlie and Jane Wu; IZA discussion paper 18945
authors: Robert Fairlie and Jane Wu; IZA discussion paper 18945
locator: Abstract; definitions and comparison results in introduction and empirical sections
summary: No statistically significant unemployment increase for recent graduates in summer 2026 relative to the paper's comparison groups and periods.
appraisal: Descriptive working paper, not proof of no AI harm. Recent graduates defined as ages 22-25 with a bachelor's degree as highest qualification and not in school. AI effects cannot be isolated from other labour-market changes.

title: Employment at Anthropic
publisher: Anthropic research; Wilmers, Catipon, Massenkoff and McCrory
authors: Anthropic research; Wilmers, Catipon, Massenkoff and McCrory
inspection_scope: Relevant article passages inspected; exact chart endpoint not independently extracted
locator: Labour demand and hiring-scorecard sections
origin_group: Company internal records, interviews and automated scorecard analysis
summary: Reports changing technical hiring emphasis towards judgment, autonomy and creative AI use, alongside a declining junior share.
appraisal: One rapidly growing AI company reporting on itself. Commercial interest and composition changes limit generalisation. Do not infer nationwide hiring requirements, older-worker superiority, or absolute junior job destruction. Numeric junior-share chart deferred until exact reference dates verified.
reference_period: Internal hiring and workforce records since 2024/early 2025, as reported October 2026
